I am 61 years old, and I have farmed the same plot in Quzhou County since I was a young bride. I never went to school, but I know this land with my hands and my eyes. My family has 3.5 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. I do not take risks with new crops because my family depends on this harvest, and the grain buyers always come for wheat and corn.

This year, just like every year, I will plant winter wheat in late October after the National Day holiday. I will buy improved wheat seeds from the local supply shop — the same kind my neighbors use, because if their fields look good, mine will too. Before planting, I will rotary till the soil to break up the corn stubble. I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and then top-dress with urea in the spring when the wheat turns green. Wheat needs water, and the sky here does not give enough, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter so the seedlings do not freeze, once at green-up, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once during grain filling. I will spray pesticide two or three times when I see aphids or rust starting.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. There is only a short window, so I will rotary till quickly and put in hybrid corn seeds — they cost more, but they grow fast and yield heavy ears. Corn needs less fuss than wheat, but I will fertilize it once at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when it is knee-high. I will irrigate it twice, at the big trumpet leaf stage and during silking, if the rains do not come. I will spray for armyworms and corn borers twice. I expect about 500 jin per mu of wheat and 600 jin per mu of corn, which is enough to feed my family and sell the rest.
